options.C: In-person verbal questioning
options.D: Face-to-face structured interview

explanation: When respondents complete the form independently without a researcher present, the opportunity for the interviewer to influence answers is removed. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T22#GNS224_U1_T22_h5)

question: What is a major limitation of relying exclusively on web-based digital questionnaires in certain developing community settings?

options.A: Excessive printing and paper costs for the research institution
options.B: Immediate mandatory requirement for face-to-face clinical trials
options.C: Complete inability to utilize closed-ended question formats
options.D: Potential exclusion of populations with limited digital access or literacy

explanation: Digital divides mean electronic surveys often miss vulnerable or rural groups who lack smartphones, internet connectivity, or technological literacy. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T22#GNS224_U1_T22_h5)

question: What is the primary purpose of conducting a pilot study for a questionnaire?

options.A: To secure permanent ethical approval from the government
options.B: To publish the final research findings ahead of schedule
options.C: To identify flaws, ambiguity, and practical issues before the main study
options.D: To substitute for the actual sample size required by statistics

explanation: Piloting tests the feasibility and clarity of the instrument so modifications can be made prior to full data collection. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T22#GNS224_U1_T22_h6)

question: What should generally be done with the data collected during the questionnaire piloting phase?

options.A: Merge it directly into the final published results
options.B: Use it exclusively to calculate participant monetary stipends
options.C: Exclude it from the final research data analysis
options.D: Publish it separately as a distinct clinical trial

explanation: Because pilot testing often leads to revisions and question adjustments, combining pilot data with final data would compromise research consistency. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T22#GNS224_U1_T22_h6)

question: Which of the following is NOT an ethical requirement for questionnaire-based research?

options.A: Protection of participant confidentiality
options.B: Voluntary informed consent from respondents
options.C: The right to withdraw at any time
options.D: Mandatory participation of all available patients

explanation: Participation in research must always be entirely voluntary, and forcing individuals to take part violates fundamental ethical research codes. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T22#GNS224_U1_T22_h7)

question: What is the key distinction between anonymity and confidentiality in survey research?

options.A: Anonymity means no identifying data is collected, while confidentiality means identifiers are protected
options.B: There is no practical difference between the two terms in clinical studies
options.C: Confidentiality applies only to digital questionnaires, whereas anonymity applies to paper
options.D: Anonymity is legally required, but confidentiality is entirely optional for nurses

explanation: An anonymous survey collects zero identifying marks, whereas a confidential survey collects names or codes but promises to keep them strictly guarded. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T22#GNS224_U1_T22_h7)

question: What is a well-documented limitation of self-reported questionnaires?

options.A: Excessive cost compared to running multi-center clinical trials
options.B: Inability to ever use closed-ended questions for analysis
options.C: Social desirability bias where respondents answer to please researchers
options.D: Mandatory requirement for continuous surgical supervision

explanation: Participants frequently tend to answer questions in a manner they perceive will be viewed favorably by healthcare staff or society. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T22#GNS224_U1_T22_h8)

question: Why might a researcher choose a questionnaire over an observational study?

options.A: To eliminate the need for any statistical software analysis
options.B: To manipulate biological variables in a controlled laboratory
options.C: To efficiently gather data on attitudes and opinions from a large group
options.D: To directly witness physical healing processes in real time

explanation: Questionnaires excel at capturing subjective internal states like beliefs and satisfaction across broad populations efficiently. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T22#GNS224_U1_T22_h8)

question: What is the primary function of a checklist in nursing research?

options.A: To replace the need for ethical approval in observational studies
options.B: To provide a narrative description of unstructured clinical events
options.C: To systematically record the presence or absence of specific items
options.D: To calculate statistical p-values automatically during data entry

explanation: Checklists use a structured format to document whether predetermined behaviors or conditions are observed or not. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T23#GNS224_U1_T23_h1)

question: Why do investigators prefer using checklists over unstructured note-taking during busy clinical observations?

options.A: They allow patients to diagnose their own clinical conditions
options.B: They completely eliminate the possibility of human recording error
options.C: They remove the requirement for informed consent in research
options.D: They minimize observer drift and personal bias by directing focus

explanation: Structured tools keep the observer focused on standardized variables, reducing subjective drift over time. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T23#GNS224_U1_T23_h1)

question: In an observational study examining sterile technique, what is a checklist typically used to record?

options.A: The financial cost of the equipment utilized during care
options.B: The long-term prognosis of the underlying medical diagnosis
options.C: The patient's subjective emotional state and coping skills
options.D: The sequence and presence of specific clinical actions

explanation: Observational checklists track whether required procedural steps are performed correctly in real-time. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T23#GNS224_U1_T23_h2)

question: How do checklists contribute to the quantitative analysis phase of a study?

options.A: By automatically generating graphical charts without software
options.B: By bypassing the need for descriptive statistical calculations
options.C: By standardizing criteria so every encounter is evaluated identically
options.D: By converting qualitative interviews into long narrative summaries

explanation: Uniform data collection allows researchers to aggregate numbers and run accurate statistical tests across the dataset. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T23#GNS224_U1_T23_h2)

question: Which type of checklist utilizes simple binary options like 'Yes' or 'No'?

options.A: Dichotomous checklist
options.B: Descriptive checklist
options.C: Scaled checklist
options.D: Frequency checklist

explanation: Dichotomous formats offer two mutually exclusive choices to record whether a criterion was met. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T23#GNS224_U1_T23_h3)

question: A researcher wants to count how many times a nurse washes their hands during a four-hour shift. Which checklist type is most appropriate?

options.A: Descriptive checklist
options.B: Frequency checklist
options.C: Dichotomous checklist
options.D: Scaled checklist

explanation: When the goal is to measure the count or occurrence rate of an action over time, a frequency checklist is selected. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T23#GNS224_U1_T23_h3)

question: What is the final step typically performed before full-scale data collection using a newly designed checklist?

options.A: Publishing the raw data in an open-access nursing journal
options.B: Conducting a pilot test in a small clinical setting
options.C: Securing immediate financial grants from the hospital board
options.D: Destroying all previous drafts of the research proposal

explanation: Pilot testing uncovers practical flaws and ambiguous items before launching the main study. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T23#GNS224_U1_T23_h4)

question: Why is expert review an essential phase in checklist construction?

options.A: To replace the need for conducting a formal literature review
options.B: To guarantee that patients consent to participate in the study
options.C: To establish content validity by evaluating item relevance
options.D: To ensure that no statistical calculations will be required

explanation: Subject matter experts review drafts to confirm that the items adequately cover the intended clinical domain. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T23#GNS224_U1_T23_h4)

question: What statistical measure is commonly used to assess inter-rater reliability between two observers using a checklist?

options.A: Pearson correlation
options.B: Cohen's kappa
options.C: Student's t-test
options.D: Chi-square test

explanation: Cohen's kappa evaluates the level of agreement between two independent raters using categorical or checklist data. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T23#GNS224_U1_T23_h5)

question: Why is inter-rater reliability particularly important when multiple research assistants use a checklist in a clinical trial?

options.A: To calculate the exact financial budget required for the study
options.B: To eliminate all forms of random patient drop-out during follow-up
options.C: To ensure different observers score the same event consistently
options.D: To prove that the sample size is large enough for generalisation

explanation: High inter-rater reliability confirms that data collectors interpret and mark checklist items in the same uniform manner. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T23#GNS224_U1_T23_h5)

question: What phenomenon occurs when clinical staff alter their normal behavior because they realize they are being observed?

options.A: Attrition bias
options.B: Observer fatigue
options.C: Hawthorne effect
options.D: Placebo response

explanation: The Hawthorne effect describes behavioral changes induced by the awareness of being watched or studied. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T23#GNS224_U1_T23_h6)

question: Which strategy helps mitigate the Hawthorne effect during clinical checklist observations?

options.A: Removing all complex items from the checklist to speed up documentation
options.B: Informing every patient of the exact hypothesis before the shift starts
options.C: Replacing all clinical staff with automated video recording software
options.D: Training observers to blend into the environment and position themselves discreetly

explanation: Discreet positioning helps staff return to natural routines, yielding more accurate observational data. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T23#GNS224_U1_T23_h6)

question: Which of the following is a recognized advantage of using checklists in healthcare research?

options.A: Fast and straightforward data collection
options.B: Complete elimination of observer bias
options.C: Automatic qualitative transcription of dialogue
options.D: Deep narrative exploration of patient feelings

explanation: Checklists allow rapid, standardized recording of structured items during busy clinical shifts. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T23#GNS224_U1_T23_h7)

question: What is a major limitation associated with structured checklist data?

options.A: They prevent researchers from publishing quantitative results
options.B: They require complex software licenses to record simple binary marks
options.C: They take significantly longer to analyze than open-ended essays
options.D: They fail to capture the underlying reasons or context behind behaviors

explanation: Because checklists focus on predefined items, they miss qualitative context and the 'why' behind an action. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T23#GNS224_U1_T23_h7)

question: What is the primary purpose of qualitative research interviews in nursing?

options.A: To capture deep insights into human experiences and perspectives
options.B: To establish numerical baseline data for hospital administration
options.C: To test specific pharmacological interventions on patient groups
options.D: To measure statistical variance across large population samples

explanation: Qualitative interviews focus on understanding subjective experiences and meanings rather than gathering numerical data for statistical testing. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T24#GNS224_U1_T24_h1)

question: How do qualitative interviews differ fundamentally from quantitative survey questionnaires?

options.A: Surveys are exclusively used in qualitative research while interviews belong to quantitative design
options.B: Interviews require larger sample sizes to achieve statistical significance than standard surveys
options.C: Interviews use flexible dialogue to explore context, whereas surveys rely on fixed, closed-ended responses
options.D: Surveys allow for emotional exploration while interviews strictly measure physiological metrics

explanation: While surveys collect standardized data using rigid metrics, interviews provide the conversational space needed to uncover complex contextual meanings. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T24#GNS224_U1_T24_h1)

question: Which interview type utilizes an interview guide with flexible open-ended prompts and core topics?

options.A: Structured interview
options.B: Unstructured interview
options.C: Semi-structured interview
options.D: Experimental interview

explanation: Semi-structured formats balance standardization and adaptability by using a guide while letting the conversation evolve naturally. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T24#GNS224_U1_T24_h2)

question: An interviewer starts a session with one broad opening statement and allows the participant to direct the entire conversation without a predefined list of questions. What type of interview is this?

options.A: Unstructured interview
options.B: Semi-structured protocol
options.C: Systematic clinical audit
options.D: Structured questionnaire

explanation: Unstructured interviews lack a rigid guide, relying instead on a single broad prompt to encourage unrestricted storytelling from the participant. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T24#GNS224_U1_T24_h2)

question: What type of questions should qualitative researchers primarily use in an interview guide?

options.A: Leading questions
options.B: Dichotomous questions
options.C: Closed-ended questions
options.D: Open-ended questions

explanation: Open-ended questions invite detailed, descriptive narratives rather than brief, restrictive responses. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T24#GNS224_U1_T24_h3)

question: Which of the following represents a poorly phrased leading question that should be avoided in research?

options.A: Don't you agree that the hospital food is terrible?
options.B: What has your experience been with hospital nutrition?
options.C: Can you describe a typical meal you received on the ward?
options.D: How do you feel about the dietary options provided here?

explanation: Leading questions push the participant toward a specific viewpoint, compromising the objectivity and authenticity of the qualitative data. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T24#GNS224_U1_T24_h3)

question: What must a researcher secure before approaching clinical units to recruit participants for a study?

options.A: Complete patient medical records
options.B: Ethical clearance or approval
options.C: Immediate financial sponsorship
options.D: Direct endorsement from hospital owners

explanation: Institutional and ethical approval is a mandatory prerequisite before any human subject recruitment can begin in a healthcare setting. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T24#GNS224_U1_T24_h4)

question: A nurse researcher wants to interview hospitalized patients on a medical ward. What is the most critical principle to emphasize during the recruitment process?

options.A: Interviewing is a mandatory requirement for receiving discharge medications
options.B: Family members must approve all statements made during the interview session
options.C: Patients must complete all interview questions to be discharged from the ward
options.D: Participation is entirely voluntary and declining will not impact their clinical care

explanation: Vulnerable patients must feel zero coercion, knowing their routine healthcare services remain completely independent of their research participation. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T24#GNS224_U1_T24_h4)

question: What is the term for a follow-up prompt used by an interviewer to encourage a participant to elaborate further?

options.A: Probe
options.B: Lead
options.C: Anchor
options.D: Directive

explanation: Probes are neutral follow-up techniques used to elicit deeper details without steering the participant's narrative. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T24#GNS224_U1_T24_h5)

question: Why is establishing psychological comfort and rapport essential during a qualitative health interview?

options.A: It transforms subjective opinions into measurable quantitative metrics
options.B: It encourages open, honest sharing of sensitive personal experiences
options.C: It eliminates the need for any subsequent data transcription
options.D: It guarantees that the participant will answer every question accurately

explanation: A strong rapport lowers defensive barriers, allowing participants to comfortably share deep emotional or clinical realities. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T24#GNS224_U1_T24_h5)

question: Which of the following best describes how participant identities are typically protected during qualitative data reporting?

options.A: Sharing raw transcripts with all clinical staff members
options.B: Using pseudonyms and removing identifying demographic details
options.C: Publishing full real names to ensure academic credit
options.D: Storing audio recordings in unsecured public cloud folders

explanation: Anonymity and confidentiality are preserved by masking real names and scrubbing identifying markers from final research outputs. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T24#GNS224_U1_T24_h6)

question: What does the concept of ongoing informed consent imply in qualitative research?

options.A: Consent is a continuous process where participants can reaffirm their willingness throughout the study
options.B: Participants sign a contract binding them to complete all interview phases
options.C: Consent is finalized once at the beginning and never needs to be revisited
options.D: Researchers can alter study protocols without notifying the participants

explanation: Informed consent extends beyond a single initial document, remaining an active, ongoing agreement between researcher and participant. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T24#GNS224_U1_T24_h6)

question: What does verbatim transcription require the researcher or transcriber to do?

options.A: Summarize the main themes while discarding minor conversational filler
options.B: Translate all local dialects into standard international medical terminology
options.C: Convert audio files directly into statistical frequency tables
options.D: Type out the spoken audio word-for-word, including non-verbal cues

explanation: Verbatim transcription captures the exact dialogue and meaningful vocal nuances needed for rigorous qualitative analysis. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T24#GNS224_U1_T24_h7)

question: Why is noting non-verbal cues like sighs or long pauses important during the transcription process?

options.A: They allow the researcher to calculate exact response times for statistical tests
options.B: They provide emotional context and depth to the spoken words
options.C: They are mandatory requirements for quantitative coding software
options.D: They serve as proof that the audio recorder was functioning correctly

explanation: Qualitative analysis relies on understanding the full communicative context, where pauses and tone often reveal underlying hesitation or emphasis. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T24#GNS224_U1_T24_h7)

question: What is the purpose of member checking in qualitative research?

options.A: To allow participants to verify the accuracy and resonance of the findings
options.B: To verify that all participants have paid their research honorariums
options.C: To check if the interview room meets environmental safety standards
options.D: To measure the physical health status of participants post-interview

explanation: Member checking enhances credibility by letting participants confirm whether the researcher's interpretations truly reflect their experiences. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T24#GNS224_U1_T24_h8)

question: Which term replaces traditional quantitative reliability in qualitative research to denote consistency across the study process?

options.A: Statistical power
options.B: Generalizability
options.C: Dependability
options.D: Objectivity index

explanation: Dependability ensures that the research process is logical, traceable, and well-documented over time, mirroring reliability in qualitative terms. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T24#GNS224_U1_T24_h8)

question: What is the primary advantage of observation over self-reported data collection methods?

options.A: It is completely free from ethical constraints
options.B: It requires minimal time from the researcher
options.C: It captures actual behavior in real time
options.D: It eliminates the need for any recording tools

explanation: Observation looks directly at actions as they happen rather than relying on what participants claim they do. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T25#GNS224_U1_T25_h1)

question: Why might a nurse researcher choose observation over questionnaires when studying patient-nurse interactions?

options.A: Observation guarantees a 100 percent response rate
options.B: Questionnaires are prone to social desirability bias
options.C: Questionnaires cost more money to print and distribute
options.D: Patients are unable to speak during hospital stays

explanation: People often report what they think sounds correct rather than their true actions, making direct observation a more accurate tool. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T25#GNS224_U1_T25_h1)

question: How is non-participant observation defined?

options.A: The study relies entirely on written questionnaires
options.B: The researcher watches events without active involvement
options.C: The investigator secretly films patients without consent
options.D: The nurse actively participates in patient care routines

explanation: In non-participant observation, the observer remains completely outside the group or setting being studied to avoid influencing the dynamics. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T25#GNS224_U1_T25_h2)

question: Which observational type is best suited for generating numeric frequencies of specific clinical behaviors?

options.A: Participant observation
options.B: Structured observation
options.C: Naturalistic observation
options.D: Unstructured observation

explanation: Structured observation utilizes predefined categories and tally systems, which easily translate into quantitative data and statistical analysis. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T25#GNS224_U1_T25_h2)

question: What is the initial step in the observational research process?

options.A: Intervening directly in emergency patient care
options.B: Defining the research question and target behaviors
options.C: Publishing the final findings in a journal
options.D: Purchasing high-definition video recording cameras

explanation: Before watching any setting, a researcher must clearly establish what they are looking for to maintain focus and accuracy. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T25#GNS224_U1_T25_h3)

question: Why is gaining approval from ward gatekeepers essential before beginning observational studies in a hospital?

options.A: It allows the researcher to direct nursing staff duties
options.B: It completely eliminates the Hawthorne effect
options.C: It guarantees that patients will recover much faster
options.D: It ensures ethical compliance and smooth operational entry

explanation: Unit managers and hospital leadership must grant formal permission to protect patient privacy and integrate the researcher safely into the clinical area. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T25#GNS224_U1_T25_h3)

question: Which tool provides a simple binary tally of whether a specific clinical action occurred?

options.A: A rating scale
options.B: A field note diary
options.C: An audio transcript
options.D: A checklist

explanation: Checklists contain explicit items where an observer simply checks off the presence or absence of a behavior. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T25#GNS224_U1_T25_h4)

question: What is the primary purpose of writing descriptive field notes during an observation session?

options.A: To grade the clinical performance of individual staff
options.B: To replace the need for institutional ethical approval
options.C: To calculate exact statistical p-values instantly
options.D: To capture contextual details and non-verbal cues

explanation: Field notes provide rich narrative context that numbers alone cannot convey, capturing the environment and subtle nuances of human interaction. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T25#GNS224_U1_T25_h4)

question: A patient changes how they speak to student nurses because they notice a researcher taking notes in the corner. What phenomenon does this illustrate?

options.A: The Hawthorne effect
options.B: Sampling error
options.C: Response fatigue
options.D: Observer bias

explanation: The Hawthorne effect describes behavioral changes that occur in human subjects solely because they are aware of being observed. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T25#GNS224_U1_T25_h5)

question: Which of the following is NOT a limitation of observational research?

options.A: Elimination of all language barriers
options.B: Vulnerability to subjective observer bias
options.C: Risk of altering behavior via observation
options.D: High consumption of time and resources

explanation: Eliminating language barriers is an advantage rather than a limitation, since observation relies on visual actions rather than spoken words. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T25#GNS224_U1_T25_h5)

question: How do researchers typically establish inter-rater reliability during structured observation?

options.A: By running a statistical test on a single observer's notes over three separate days
options.B: By ensuring the hospital management approves the study protocol in writing
options.C: By having multiple observers independently score the same session and comparing results
options.D: By asking patients to rate the accuracy of the researcher's field notes afterward

explanation: Comparing scores from separate observers ensures that the measurement tool is objective and free from individual personal bias. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T25#GNS224_U1_T25_h6)

question: Why does covert observation present significant ethical challenges in nursing research?

options.A: It makes statistical data analysis completely impossible to perform
options.B: It guarantees that the Hawthorne effect will completely ruin the study
options.C: It violates the principle of autonomy by failing to obtain informed consent
options.D: It always causes physical harm to vulnerable hospitalized patients

explanation: Watching individuals without their knowledge strips them of their right to choose whether or not to participate in a research study. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T25#GNS224_U1_T25_h6)

question: What does validity primarily determine in a research study?

options.A: The total number of participants recruited for the clinical trial
options.B: The degree to which an instrument measures what it is intended to measure
options.C: The statistical software used to analyze the collected data
options.D: The consistency of scores obtained over repeated measurements

explanation: Validity specifically evaluates the truthfulness and accuracy of an investigative tool or study design in capturing the true phenomenon under study. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T26#GNS224_U1_T26_h1)

question: Why is establishing research validity particularly critical for clinical nursing practice?

options.A: Hospital administrators require valid scores to evaluate nurse staffing levels
options.B: Flawed evidence can directly compromise patient safety and care outcomes
options.C: It guarantees that research funding will be renewed for subsequent years
options.D: Regulatory boards mandate validity checks before equipment purchase

explanation: Because clinical protocols stem from research findings, poor validity can result in incorrect patient interventions and compromised health outcomes. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T26#GNS224_U1_T26_h1)

question: What is the primary focus of internal validity in a research study?

options.A: Calculating precise p-values using advanced software
options.B: Applying study results to diverse patient populations globally
options.C: Establishing a true cause-and-effect relationship between variables
options.D: Ensuring participants answer survey questions honestly

explanation: Internal validity is concerned with ruling out alternative explanations to confirm that the intervention truly caused the observed outcome. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T26#GNS224_U1_T26_h2)

question: Which methodological approach is most effective for strengthening the internal validity of an experimental study?

options.A: Random assignment of participants to experimental and control groups
options.B: Allowing individuals to choose their preferred study group
options.C: Increasing the total geographic spread of the recruitment centers
options.D: Selecting participants who already support the hypothesis

explanation: Random assignment distributes confounding variables evenly between groups, ensuring that baseline differences do not skew the causal conclusions. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T26#GNS224_U1_T26_h2)

question: What does external validity evaluate in healthcare research?

options.A: The statistical significance of the primary outcome measure
options.B: The generalizability of findings to other settings and populations
options.C: The accuracy of the laboratory equipment used to test blood samples
options.D: The ability of the researcher to control extraneous environmental variables

explanation: External validity addresses whether conclusions drawn from a sample can safely apply to broader, real-world populations and environments. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T26#GNS224_U1_T26_h3)

question: A research study recruits participants exclusively from a single private hospital with high-tech equipment. Which validity type is most directly threatened by this selection bias?

options.A: Internal validity
options.B: Statistical conclusion validity
options.C: External validity
options.D: Construct validity

explanation: Using a single, highly specialized sample limits the ability to generalize the results to standard public hospitals or resource-limited settings. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T26#GNS224_U1_T26_h3)

question: What is the primary purpose of construct validity?

options.A: Determining whether an instrument accurately measures an abstract theoretical concept
options.B: Checking if mathematical calculations in the results section are free from error
options.C: Ensuring that the study sample size is large enough to detect a real effect
options.D: Evaluating whether findings can be applied across different clinical hospitals

explanation: Construct validity ensures that operationalized tools truly capture invisible, theoretical phenomena like fatigue, stress, or intelligence. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T26#GNS224_U1_T26_h4)

question: When a researcher compares a new depression screening tool against an established, widely accepted diagnostic scale, which type of validity is being tested?

options.A: Internal validity
options.B: Criterion validity
options.C: Discriminant validity
options.D: External validity

explanation: Criterion validity evaluates a new tool by comparing its performance directly against an established, reliable gold standard. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T26#GNS224_U1_T26_h4)

question: What does the term 'attrition' refer to as a threat to research validity?

options.A: The gradual wearing down and recalibration failure of physical medical devices
options.B: The sudden occurrence of a major external historical event during a trial
options.C: The natural fatigue experienced by researchers during long data collection shifts
options.D: The loss of study participants over the course of a longitudinal investigation

explanation: Attrition happens when participants drop out over time, leaving a potentially biased subset who completed the entire study. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T26#GNS224_U1_T26_h5)

question: Which scenario describes the validity threat known as maturation?

options.A: Observers scoring patient anxiety levels become more lenient by the end of the data collection period
options.B: A sudden power outage at the clinic ruins laboratory blood samples stored in a standard refrigerator
options.C: Half of the nurses enrolled in a stress-reduction study resign and leave the hospital mid-trial
options.D: Elderly patients show improved cognitive test scores simply because they grew accustomed to the testing format over time

explanation: Maturation involves natural physiological or psychological changes, including learning effects, that occur within participants as time passes. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T26#GNS224_U1_T26_h5)

question: What is the primary goal of critically appraising published nursing literature?

options.A: To check if the article has been cited by other international authors
options.B: To determine if a study's validity supports integrating its findings into clinical practice
options.C: To ensure the reference list complies with standard academic formatting rules
options.D: To verify that the authors received adequate financial grants for their research

explanation: Critical appraisal helps nurses sift through published evidence to find methodologically sound studies that can safely guide patient care. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T26#GNS224_U1_T26_h6)

question: Which section of a research report provides the most crucial details for evaluating a study's internal and external validity?

options.A: References
options.B: Acknowledgements
options.C: Introduction
options.D: Methodology

explanation: The methodology section outlines how the study was conducted, including sampling, controls, and instruments, which directly determines validity. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T26#GNS224_U1_T26_h6)

question: What primary characteristic does a reliable research instrument demonstrate?

options.A: Consistency of scores over repeated measurements
options.B: Freedom from all forms of systematic bias
options.C: Generalizability across different patient populations
options.D: Accuracy in measuring the intended theoretical concept

explanation: Reliability is fundamentally defined by consistency and repeatability when the same measurement is taken multiple times. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T27#GNS224_U1_T27_h1)

question: How does random error impact a clinical measurement tool?

options.A: It directly decreases the instrument's reliability
options.B: It shifts all measured scores in a predictable direction
options.C: It improves the overall validity of the study findings
options.D: It eliminates the need for statistical significance testing

explanation: Random error introduces unpredictable fluctuations in scores, which reduces the consistency and overall reliability of the tool. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T27#GNS224_U1_T27_h1)

question: Which statement correctly contrasts validity and reliability in research instruments?

options.A: Reliability requires random error, while validity requires systematic error
options.B: Reliability assesses consistency, while validity assesses accuracy
options.C: Validity measures stability, while reliability measures bias
options.D: Validity focuses on sample size, while reliability focuses on data collection

explanation: Reliability checks if results can be repeated, whereas validity checks if the tool actually measures the intended concept. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T27#GNS224_U1_T27_h2)

question: A clinical scale consistently yields the exact same incorrect score for a patient's anxiety level. What is the measurement property of this tool?

options.A: Low reliability and high validity
options.B: Both low reliability and low validity
options.C: High reliability and low validity
options.D: Both high reliability and high validity

explanation: Consistency gives it high reliability, but because the score is wrong, it fails to measure the true concept, indicating low validity. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T27#GNS224_U1_T27_h2)

question: What does test-retest reliability primarily measure?

options.A: Stability of scores over time
options.B: Homogeneity of items within a single scale
options.C: Equivalence between two alternative test versions
options.D: Agreement between two different observers

explanation: Test-retest reliability administers the same test twice to evaluate whether scores remain stable across a time interval. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T27#GNS224_U1_T27_h3)

question: Why is choosing an appropriate time interval critical when conducting a test-retest reliability study?

options.A: Short intervals prevent researchers from using Pearson correlation coefficients
options.B: Extended time gaps reduce the sample size required for correlation analysis
options.C: Too long an interval ensures participants will drop out of the study completely
options.D: Too short an interval can lead to memory effects that falsely elevate scores

explanation: If retested too quickly, respondents remember past answers, making the tool appear more reliable than it actually is. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T27#GNS224_U1_T27_h3)

question: What is the minimum acceptable threshold for Cronbach's alpha in most established nursing research studies?
explanation: A Cronbach's alpha coefficient of 0.70 or higher is widely accepted as indicating adequate internal consistency for a scale. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T27#GNS224_U1_T27_h4)

question: When is a researcher most likely to use the Kuder-Richardson 20 formula instead of Cronbach's alpha?

options.A: When administering parallel forms of an assessment instrument
options.B: When comparing ratings provided by two different clinical observers
options.C: When scale items are dichotomous, such as true/false questions
options.D: When evaluating stability over an extended time interval

explanation: KR-20 is mathematically designed for tests containing items with two possible answers, like correct versus incorrect. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T27#GNS224_U1_T27_h4)

question: What does inter-rater reliability assess?

options.A: The degree of agreement between different observers using the same tool
options.B: The stability of a questionnaire administered twice to the same patients
options.C: The internal homogeneity of items within a single observational scale
options.D: The correlation between two different versions of a clinical examination

explanation: Inter-rater reliability measures how consistently separate judges or observers score the same events or patients. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T27#GNS224_U1_T27_h5)

question: Two nursing students independently evaluate a patient's wound healing stage using a standardized staging tool. Which type of reliability are researchers testing when comparing their scores?

options.A: Test-retest reliability
options.B: Inter-rater reliability
options.C: Parallel forms reliability
options.D: Intra-rater reliability

explanation: Comparing independent evaluations made by two separate people at the same time tests inter-rater reliability. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T27#GNS224_U1_T27_h5)

question: What is the primary purpose of parallel forms reliability?

options.A: To determine if all questions within a single test measure the same concept
options.B: To compare scores from two equivalent versions of the same test
options.C: To evaluate whether a clinical scale remains stable over several weeks
options.D: To measure how consistently a single observer rates a patient over time

explanation: Parallel forms reliability examines the correlation between two distinct yet equivalent versions of an assessment tool. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T27#GNS224_U1_T27_h6)

question: Which measurement challenge does the use of parallel forms reliability help overcome?

options.A: Low internal consistency resulting from poorly worded survey questions
options.B: Variability caused by different nurses scoring the same patient behavior
options.C: Systematic bias introduced by faulty medical equipment calibration
options.D: Practice or memory effects from taking the exact same test twice

explanation: Because participants take a different set of equivalent items on the second test, they cannot simply recall their previous answers. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T27#GNS224_U1_T27_h6)

question: Why is it insufficient for authors to rely solely on published reliability estimates from previous studies?

options.A: Published reliability statistics automatically expire after a five-year period
options.B: Ethics committees prohibit the citation of historical psychometric data
options.C: Previous researchers always calculate Cronbach's alpha incorrectly
options.D: Reliability can vary significantly across different sample populations and settings

explanation: Psychometric properties are sample-dependent, meaning a tool may perform differently in a new study population. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T27#GNS224_U1_T27_h7)

question: Which of the following research practices is NOT recommended when reporting instrument reliability?

options.A: Discussing potential measurement errors that could have affected data collection
options.B: Ensuring chosen coefficients match the specific type of data collected
options.C: Citing old validation studies without testing reliability in the current sample
options.D: Reporting specific Cronbach's alpha values for every scale utilized in the study

explanation: Researchers must calculate and report reliability for their own specific sample rather than assuming past validation is enough. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T27#GNS224_U1_T27_h7)

question: What is the primary function of a research design in a nursing study?

options.A: Determining the exact cost of conducting the project
options.B: Recruiting eligible human participants for the trial
options.C: Providing a detailed literature review for the background
options.D: Acting as a structural blueprint to guide the entire study

explanation: Research design acts as the master plan or blueprint that directs how a study is executed from start to finish. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T3#GNS224_U1_T3_h1)

question: Why is minimizing extraneous variables through a solid design critical for clinical evidence?

options.A: It bypasses the requirement for institutional ethical approval
options.B: It ensures that the observed outcomes are genuinely due to the independent variable
options.C: It eliminates the need for statistical data analysis software
options.D: It guarantees immediate funding from international health organizations

explanation: Controlling external factors helps establish cause-and-effect relationships with higher internal validity. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T3#GNS224_U1_T3_h1)

question: What type of data is primarily collected in quantitative research designs?

options.A: Historical diaries
options.B: Narrative text
options.C: Audio transcripts
options.D: Numerical data

explanation: Quantitative research fundamentally relies on numbers and statistical metrics to measure variables. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T3#GNS224_U1_T3_h2)

question: A researcher wants to study the statistical relationship between years of clinical experience and frequency of documentation errors among nurses. Which design fits best?

options.A: Correlational quantitative
options.B: Phenomenological qualitative
options.C: Experimental intervention
options.D: Historical case study

explanation: Correlational designs are used to examine relationships between variables without actively manipulating them. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T3#GNS224_U1_T3_h2)

question: What is the main purpose of qualitative research designs in healthcare?

options.A: Calculating population disease prevalence rates
options.B: Establishing definitive cause-and-effect drug dosages
options.C: Measuring exact biochemical levels in blood samples
options.D: Exploring subjective human experiences and meanings

explanation: Qualitative designs prioritize understanding the rich, personal perspectives of individuals. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T3#GNS224_U1_T3_h3)

question: Which qualitative approach specifically aims to immerse a researcher within a distinct cultural group to study their behaviors?

options.A: Experimental
options.B: Correlational
options.C: Phenomenology
options.D: Ethnography

explanation: Ethnographic studies involve cultural immersion to observe and document shared patterns of behavior and belief. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T3#GNS224_U1_T3_h3)

question: What feature is present in true experimental designs that is typically missing in quasi-experimental designs?

options.A: Formulation of a testable research hypothesis
options.B: Measurement of an independent variable
options.C: Random assignment of participants to groups
options.D: Collection of numerical measurement data

explanation: Random assignment is the defining hallmark that separates true experiments from quasi-experiments. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T3#GNS224_U1_T3_h4)

question: A nurse researcher wants to test a new wound care protocol across two existing hospital wards without disrupting current staff assignments or randomly mixing patients. Which design is most appropriate?

options.A: Quasi-experimental
options.B: True randomized controlled trial
options.C: Phenomenological interview
options.D: Pure descriptive survey

explanation: When random assignment is impossible due to existing organizational structures, a quasi-experimental design is used. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T3#GNS224_U1_T3_h4)

question: What is a defining characteristic of non-experimental research designs?

options.A: Absence of manipulation of the independent variable
options.B: Mandatory random assignment of human subjects
options.C: Exclusive use of qualitative narrative interviews
options.D: Direct clinical testing of pharmacological agents

explanation: Non-experimental research observes phenomena naturally without the researcher introducing any active interventions. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T3#GNS224_U1_T3_h5)

question: Which design collects data from a study population at one specific point in time to provide a snapshot of current conditions?

options.A: Longitudinal cohort design
options.B: Randomized controlled trial
options.C: Cross-sectional design
options.D: Grounded theory study

explanation: Cross-sectional studies measure variables simultaneously at a single point in time. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T3#GNS224_U1_T3_h5)

question: What does a mixed methods research design combine within a single study?

options.A: Laboratory and animal testing protocols
options.B: Primary and secondary literature reviews
options.C: Quantitative and qualitative data
options.D: Inpatient and outpatient funding sources

explanation: Mixed methods deliberately integrate both numerical and narrative research approaches. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T3#GNS224_U1_T3_h6)

question: In an explanatory sequential mixed methods study, which phase is conducted FIRST?

options.A: Qualitative thematic narrative coding
options.B: Simultaneous triangulation of results
options.C: Instrument development based on interviews
options.D: Quantitative data collection and analysis

explanation: In an explanatory sequential design, the quantitative phase comes first, followed by a qualitative phase to help explain those numbers. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T3#GNS224_U1_T3_h6)

question: Which factor is considered the primary driver when selecting a research design?

options.A: The availability of high-speed computer printers
options.B: The personal preference of the funding agency
options.C: The total number of pages in the final report
options.D: The specific nature of the research question

explanation: The research question dictates whether you need to measure numbers, explore meanings, or test causes. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T3#GNS224_U1_T3_h7)

question: Why might a researcher choose an observational design over an experimental design for studying a harmful environmental exposure?

options.A: It is unethical to intentionally expose human subjects to harmful agents
options.B: Experimental designs cannot produce any statistically valid data
options.C: Institutional review boards require experiments to be avoided
options.D: Observational designs always cost more money than clinical trials

explanation: Ethical principles prohibit researchers from inflicting potential harm on participants, ruling out experimental manipulation for dangerous exposures. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T3#GNS224_U1_T3_h7)

question: What is the primary purpose of quantitative research design?

options.A: To explore deep subjective lived experiences through prolonged interviews
options.B: To generate new grounded theories from unstructured observational field notes
options.C: To document historical timelines of healthcare policy implementation
options.D: To test objective theories through statistical measurement of variables

explanation: Quantitative research relies on numerical data and statistical analysis to evaluate predetermined hypotheses and objective theories. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T4#GNS224_U1_T4_h1)

question: Why is a structured research design essential in nursing quantitative studies?

options.A: It removes the need for formal ethical board approval prior to data collection
options.B: It allows findings to be generalized from a sample to a broader population
options.C: It eliminates all possible human recording errors in clinical settings
options.D: It guarantees that patients will experience improved health outcomes

explanation: A rigorous design ensures that the data collected can be soundly analyzed and applied beyond the immediate study participants. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T4#GNS224_U1_T4_h1)

question: Which reasoning process is primarily utilized in quantitative research?

options.A: Inductive reasoning building purely from unstructured observations
options.B: Deductive reasoning starting from established theories
options.C: Abductive reasoning guessing causes from incomplete evidence
options.D: Intuitive reasoning based entirely on clinical nursing experience

explanation: Quantitative research typically begins with a general theory and tests specific hypotheses derived from it. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T4#GNS224_U1_T4_h2)

question: What is the main function of control within a quantitative research design?

options.A: To eliminate the influence of confounding extraneous variables
options.B: To prevent participants from withdrawing from the study prematurely
options.C: To ensure all participants receive the active experimental treatment
options.D: To speed up the institutional ethical review board approval process

explanation: Controlling extraneous variables ensures that changes observed in the dependent variable are genuinely caused by the independent variable. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T4#GNS224_U1_T4_h2)

question: Which of the following is REQUIRED for a study to be classified as a true experimental design?

options.A: Retrospective chart review methods
options.B: Absence of any control group
options.C: Random assignment of participants
options.D: Qualitative interviews with participants

explanation: Random assignment, along with manipulation and control, is a mandatory pillar of true experimental designs. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T4#GNS224_U1_T4_h3)

question: A nurse researcher wants to test whether a new structured mobilization protocol reduces postoperative deep vein thrombosis. What is the most rigorous design to use?

options.A: Descriptive non-experimental cross-sectional survey
options.B: Qualitative phenomenological patient interview
options.C: Retrospective case series without comparison
options.D: True experimental randomized controlled trial

explanation: Randomized controlled trials provide the highest level of experimental control needed to confirm cause-and-effect relationships. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T4#GNS224_U1_T4_h3)

question: What is the primary difference between true experimental and quasi-experimental designs?

options.A: True experimental designs are only conducted in laboratories
options.B: Quasi-experimental designs never manipulate variables
options.C: True experimental designs cannot use control groups
options.D: Quasi-experimental designs lack random assignment

explanation: Quasi-experiments manipulate the independent variable but use convenience or existing groups instead of randomisation. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T4#GNS224_U1_T4_h4)

question: Why might a nurse researcher choose a quasi-experimental design over a true experimental design?

options.A: It requires no statistical analysis or data interpretation software
options.B: It guarantees that the hypothesis will always be proven correct
options.C: It is impossible or unethical to randomly assign patients to certain groups
options.D: It completely eliminates all threats to internal research validity

explanation: Clinical realities often prevent randomisation, making quasi-experimental designs a practical and ethical alternative. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T4#GNS224_U1_T4_h4)

question: What is a defining feature of non-experimental research designs?

options.A: Absence of manipulation of the independent variable
options.B: Inability to use statistical analysis software
options.C: Mandatory random assignment of human subjects
options.D: Exclusive reliance on laboratory intervention settings

explanation: Non-experimental research observes variables as they naturally occur without introducing any active intervention or treatment. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T4#GNS224_U1_T4_h5)

question: A study measures both the caffeine intake and blood pressure levels of night-shift nurses at one single point in time. What type of design is this?

options.A: Cross-sectional correlational design
options.B: True experimental randomized trial
options.C: Quasi-experimental intervention study
options.D: Longitudinal qualitative case study

explanation: Collecting data at one point in time to examine the relationship between variables without manipulation classifies it as a cross-sectional correlational study. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T4#GNS224_U1_T4_h5)

question: What does the dependent variable represent in a quantitative study?

options.A: The active intervention or manipulation applied by the researcher
options.B: The demographic baseline characteristic of the sample population
options.C: The measured outcome or effect resulting from an intervention
options.D: The confounding factor that is intentionally ignored during analysis

explanation: The dependent variable is what the researcher measures to see the effect produced by the independent variable. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T4#GNS224_U1_T4_h6)

question: Which measurement scale categorizes data into mutually exclusive groups with a meaningful mathematical zero point?

options.A: Nominal scale
options.B: Interval scale
options.C: Ratio scale
options.D: Ordinal scale

explanation: The ratio scale possesses all properties of lower scales plus an absolute zero point, allowing for absolute comparisons. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T4#GNS224_U1_T4_h6)

question: What does instrument reliability primarily evaluate?

options.A: The consistency and stability of measurement scores over repeated use
options.B: The absence of systematic bias in experimental group allocation
options.C: The degree to which findings can be generalised to other hospitals
options.D: Whether the tool measures the exact theoretical concept intended

explanation: Reliability is all about consistency, meaning the instrument gives similar results under consistent conditions. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T4#GNS224_U1_T4_h7)

question: Which type of validity is most directly threatened if a clinical research study has severe confounding extraneous variables?

options.A: Instrument validity
options.B: External validity
options.C: Content validity
options.D: Internal validity

explanation: Internal validity examines whether the experimental treatment truly caused the outcome, which is directly undermined by confounding variables. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T4#GNS224_U1_T4_h7)

question: What is the primary purpose of securing informed consent in quantitative research?

options.A: To guarantee that participants will receive financial compensation
options.B: To legally protect the hospital from all clinical malpractice claims
options.C: To prevent patients from dropping out of experimental treatments
options.D: To ensure participants understand risks and voluntarily agree to join

explanation: Informed consent operationalises participant autonomy by ensuring full disclosure of study details before voluntary enrollment. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T4#GNS224_U1_T4_h8)

question: Which of the following groups is typically classified as vulnerable and requires special ethical protection in nursing studies?

options.A: Healthy adult university students volunteering for a survey
options.B: Experienced clinical nursing lecturers grading student papers
options.C: Licensed professional registered nurses working day shifts
options.D: Adult psychiatric patients admitted to an inpatient ward

explanation: Vulnerable populations include individuals with diminished autonomy or compromised cognitive capacity, such as psychiatric patients, requiring heightened safeguards. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T4#GNS224_U1_T4_h8)

question: What is the primary focus of qualitative research design in nursing?

options.A: Testing pre-determined clinical hypotheses in a laboratory
options.B: Understanding the meaning people give to their lived experiences
options.C: Determining the exact numerical prevalence of a disease
options.D: Measuring statistical relationships between health variables

explanation: Qualitative research is fundamentally designed to explore human experiences, perceptions, and the meanings individuals attach to health and illness. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T5#GNS224_U1_T5_h1)

question: Why is qualitative research considered inductive rather than deductive?

options.A: It builds from specific observations up to broad themes
options.B: It always begins with a rigid statistical hypothesis
options.C: It relies heavily on randomized controlled trials
options.D: It uses mathematical formulas to deduce patient outcomes

explanation: Inductive reasoning moves from detailed particulars toward general patterns or themes, which is the standard trajectory of qualitative analysis. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T5#GNS224_U1_T5_h1)

question: What philosophical term refers to the study of being and the nature of reality?

options.A: Methodology
options.B: Epistemology
options.C: Ontology
options.D: Taxonomy

explanation: Ontology deals with what exists in the world and the fundamental nature of reality as perceived by the researcher and participants. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T5#GNS224_U1_T5_h2)

question: Which paradigm is most appropriate if a nurse researcher aims to uncover how societal power imbalances affect patient care access?

options.A: Critical social theory
options.B: Descriptive epidemiology
options.C: Quantitative positivism
options.D: Strict biological determinism

explanation: Critical social theory specifically targets power dynamics, systemic oppression, and the pursuit of social justice within health contexts. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T5#GNS224_U1_T5_h2)

question: Which qualitative approach is specifically designed to generate a theory rooted in data about a social process?

options.A: Phenomenology
options.B: Historical research
options.C: Ethnography
options.D: Grounded theory

explanation: Grounded theory systematically collects and analyzes data to construct an explanatory social theory directly from the field. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T5#GNS224_U1_T5_h3)

question: A nurse researcher wants to explore the shared cultural behaviors, unwritten rules, and rituals of nurses working in a high-stress trauma center. Which methodology fits best?

options.A: Phenomenology
options.B: Ethnography
options.C: Quantitative survey
options.D: Clinical trial

explanation: Ethnography is the study of cultural groups, behaviors, and social patterns through prolonged immersion and observation. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T5#GNS224_U1_T5_h3)

question: What is the primary guiding principle for determining sample size in qualitative research?

options.A: Data saturation
options.B: Randomization tables
options.C: Population census data
options.D: Power calculation software

explanation: Qualitative studies continue sampling until data saturation is reached, meaning further data collection yields no new insights or themes. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T5#GNS224_U1_T5_h4)

question: Why is purposive sampling preferred over random sampling in qualitative nursing studies?

options.A: It intentionally selects participants with rich experience of the phenomenon
options.B: It allows the sample size to be calculated using standard mathematical formulas
options.C: It eliminates all forms of researcher bias during data collection
options.D: It ensures findings can be generalized to the entire global population

explanation: Purposive sampling ensures that the individuals chosen can actually provide deep, relevant insights into the specific research question. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T5#GNS224_U1_T5_h4)

question: What type of interview guide is most commonly used in qualitative in-depth interviews?

options.A: Semi-structured with open-ended questions
options.B: Completely random questions with no predetermined focus
options.C: Standardized diagnostic questionnaires
options.D: Strictly structured with fixed-choice answers

explanation: Semi-structured guides provide a framework of topics while allowing flexibility to follow up on participant narratives. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T5#GNS224_U1_T5_h5)

question: What is a major advantage of using focus groups over individual interviews in nursing research?

options.A: It ensures absolute confidentiality regarding sensitive medical diagnoses
options.B: It completely prevents dominant participants from talking too much
options.C: Group interaction stimulates shared perspectives and debate among peers
options.D: It is much easier to transcribe audio recordings of multiple speakers

explanation: Focus groups leverage group dynamics, allowing participants to react to, build upon, or challenge each other's ideas. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T5#GNS224_U1_T5_h5)

question: Which concept in qualitative research corresponds roughly to external validity in quantitative research?

options.A: Dependability
options.B: Confirmability
options.C: Transferability
options.D: Credibility

explanation: Transferability refers to the degree to which qualitative findings can be transferred or generalized to other settings or groups. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T5#GNS224_U1_T5_h6)

question: What is the primary purpose of maintaining an audit trail during a qualitative study?

options.A: To ensure dependability by creating a transparent record of research decisions
options.B: To restrict public access to sensitive patient health records
options.C: To calculate the exact statistical error margin of interview transcripts
options.D: To prove that all participants were paid financial compensation

explanation: An audit trail allows external reviewers to follow the researcher's logic and decisions, establishing dependability and rigor. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T5#GNS224_U1_T5_h6)

question: What is the initial step typically performed by a researcher during qualitative data analysis?

options.A: Publishing the final research manuscript in a journal
options.B: Deleting all raw audio recordings to save storage
options.C: Running a multi-variable regression analysis in SPSS
options.D: Immersion through reading and re-reading transcripts

explanation: Before coding or categorizing, the researcher must immerse themselves in the text to grasp the overall context and depth. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T5#GNS224_U1_T5_h7)

question: In qualitative analysis, what is the relationship between codes and themes?

options.A: Codes are grouped together to form broader overarching themes
options.B: Codes and themes represent entirely unrelated analytical steps
options.C: Themes are broken down into smaller mathematical codes
options.D: Themes are created first, followed by manual coding of numbers

explanation: Researchers organize specific coded segments of text into cohesive clusters that represent overarching themes in the data. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T5#GNS224_U1_T5_h7)

question: What is 'deductive disclosure' in the context of qualitative research ethics?

options.A: The mathematical deduction of a statistical p-value from interview notes
options.B: The legal requirement to report child abuse discovered during a study
options.C: The accidental identification of a participant through unique descriptive details
options.D: The formal withdrawal of a participant from an active research trial

explanation: Deductive disclosure occurs when readers piece together contextual clues to identify a specific participant despite using a pseudonym. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T5#GNS224_U1_T5_h8)

question: Why is informed consent viewed as an ongoing process in qualitative research rather than a single event?

options.A: Participants are required to sign a new consent form every single day
options.B: IRB rules mandate that financial payments are distributed incrementally
options.C: Patients often forget they are being recorded after the first hour
options.D: The direction and depth of the study evolve as data collection unfolds

explanation: Because qualitative inquiry is flexible and exploratory, participants need ongoing updates about what topics are being explored as the study progresses. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T5#GNS224_U1_T5_h8)

question: What does a research paradigm primarily establish for a nurse investigator?

options.A: Worldviews regarding truth and reality
options.B: Institutional review board approval steps
options.C: Budgetary constraints for clinical trials
options.D: The exact sample size required for a study

explanation: A paradigm dictates the fundamental assumptions an investigator holds about reality and how knowledge is acquired. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T6#GNS224_U1_T6_h1)

question: Why must the choice of a research design align with the research question?

options.A: Funding bodies strictly prohibit mixing different types of clinical research questions
options.B: Different clinical inquiries require distinct philosophical and methodological approaches
options.C: Hospital ethics committees mandate quantitative methods for patient care studies
options.D: Qualitative designs are scientifically inferior and need quantitative justification

explanation: The nature of the question dictates whether numeric measurement or narrative depth is needed to uncover the answer. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T6#GNS224_U1_T6_h1)

question: Which philosophical perspective underpins quantitative research?

options.A: Constructivism
options.B: Positivism
options.C: Phenomenology
options.D: Interpretivism

explanation: Quantitative research is rooted in positivism, which assumes that an objective reality can be measured and quantified. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T6#GNS224_U1_T6_h2)

question: What is the primary purpose of controlling variables in a quantitative study?

options.A: To make the research process entirely subjective
options.B: To minimize bias and isolate the relationship between variables
options.C: To eliminate the need for statistical analysis software
options.D: To ensure that participants do not drop out of the study

explanation: Strict control helps researchers establish cause-and-effect relationships or accurate associations without confounding factors interfering. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T6#GNS224_U1_T6_h2)

question: What is the primary type of data gathered in qualitative research?

options.A: Numerical measurements
options.B: Words and narratives
options.C: Laboratory biomarker levels
options.D: Statistical percentages

explanation: Qualitative research focuses on gathering text-based data such as interview transcripts, field notes, and open-ended narratives. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T6#GNS224_U1_T6_h3)

question: A researcher wants to deeply understand the lived experience of mothers caring for children with severe sickle cell anemia in a local clinic. Which design is most appropriate?

options.A: Descriptive epidemiological survey
options.B: Qualitative research
options.C: Randomized controlled trial
options.D: Quantitative correlational study

explanation: Investigating subjective human experiences and coping mechanisms requires a qualitative approach rather than numerical tracking. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T6#GNS224_U1_T6_h3)

question: Which of the following is a standard data collection instrument in quantitative research?

options.A: Unstructured open-ended conversational interviews
options.B: Reflective personal journals written by researchers
options.C: Extended participant observation field notes
options.D: Structured questionnaires with closed-ended items

explanation: Quantitative studies require standardized instruments that yield numeric data for statistical analysis. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T6#GNS224_U1_T6_h4)

question: How does data collection flexibility differ between the two designs?

options.A: Quantitative tools can be altered mid-study, whereas qualitative protocols are strictly unchangeable
options.B: Both designs require absolute rigidity in questionnaire wording throughout the study
options.C: Neither design permits any adjustments once the institutional review board approves the protocol
options.D: Qualitative methods allow questions to shift as insights emerge, while quantitative tools remain fixed

explanation: Qualitative data collection is iterative, allowing the researcher to pursue unexpected themes during interviews. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T6#GNS224_U1_T6_h4)

question: What is the primary tool used to analyze quantitative data?

options.A: Literary content critique
options.B: Reflective diary summaries
options.C: Statistical software packages
options.D: Thematic coding matrices

explanation: Quantitative data analysis relies heavily on statistical computations and software programs to process numbers. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T6#GNS224_U1_T6_h5)

question: Which characteristic best describes qualitative data analysis?

options.A: Calculating correlation coefficients and p-values
options.B: Testing null hypotheses via mathematical formulas
options.C: Determining statistical significance across large samples
options.D: Coding transcripts to identify recurrent themes

explanation: Qualitative analysis breaks text down into codes and categories to build a comprehensive thematic picture. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T6#GNS224_U1_T6_h5)

question: Which terms are used to evaluate the rigor of a quantitative study?

options.A: Validity and reliability
options.B: Credibility and transferability
options.C: Dependability and confirmability
options.D: Auditability and saturation

explanation: Quantitative research measures quality through validity and reliability metrics. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T6#GNS224_U1_T6_h6)

question: What is the purpose of member checking in qualitative research?

options.A: To calculate the statistical reliability coefficient of interview questions
options.B: To ensure that all research participants paid their hospital bills
options.C: To measure the exact numerical duration of each interview session
options.D: To verify the accuracy and credibility of interpreted data with participants

explanation: Member checking enhances trustworthiness by allowing participants to confirm whether research findings genuinely reflect their experiences. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T6#GNS224_U1_T6_h6)

question: What type of sample is typically sought in qualitative research?

options.A: Large, randomly selected samples for statistical power
options.B: Convenience samples restricted to hospitalized patients
options.C: Small, purposeful samples selected for deep insight
options.D: Entire regional populations to ensure absolute parity

explanation: Qualitative studies purposely select information-rich participants until data saturation is reached. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T6#GNS224_U1_T6_h7)

question: A nurse researcher wants to know both the healing rate of pressure ulcers under a new dressing and the patients' personal comfort levels during dressing changes. What research approach is most suitable?

options.A: A purely quantitative trial ignoring patient comfort feedback entirely
options.B: A mixed-methods approach combining quantitative measurement and qualitative interviews
options.C: An observational audit focusing only on nursing documentation compliance
options.D: A strictly qualitative case study measuring ulcer surface area via interviews

explanation: Combining both paradigms allows the researcher to measure clinical outcomes while capturing the subjective patient experience. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T6#GNS224_U1_T6_h7)

question: What is the primary purpose of an experimental research design in healthcare?

options.A: To observe natural behaviors without any researcher interference
options.B: To explore the subjective lived experiences of patients
options.C: To establish cause-and-effect relationships between variables
options.D: To describe the frequency of a disease in a population

explanation: Experimental designs actively manipulate variables to determine if an intervention directly causes a specific clinical outcome. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T7#GNS224_U1_T7_h1)

question: How does experimental research differ fundamentally from observational research?

options.A: Experimental research relies entirely on qualitative data collection methods
options.B: Observational research allows for strict control over confounding variables
options.C: Experimental research actively introduces an intervention, whereas observational research does not
options.D: Observational research always involves human subjects, while experimental research does not

explanation: Researchers conducting experiments introduce a treatment or change, whereas observational studies simply watch and record natural occurrences. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T7#GNS224_U1_T7_h1)

question: Which component is considered one of the three core elements of a true experimental design?

options.A: Naturalistic observation
options.B: Retrospective data collection
options.C: Phenomenological coding
options.D: Random assignment

explanation: True experiments require random assignment along with manipulation and control to reduce bias. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T7#GNS224_U1_T7_h2)

question: What is the main function of random assignment in an experimental study?

options.A: To guarantee that the sample size is large enough for statistical power
options.B: Eliminating the need for a control or comparison group
options.C: Informing participants about the potential risks of the intervention
options.D: To ensure baseline characteristics are evenly distributed between groups

explanation: Random assignment spreads confounding traits equally across study arms, preventing pre-existing group differences from affecting the results. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T7#GNS224_U1_T7_h2)

question: Which design lacks both random assignment and a control group?

options.A: Quasi-experimental design
options.B: Pre-experimental design
options.C: True experimental design
options.D: Randomized controlled trial

explanation: Pre-experimental designs offer minimal control and typically lack both random assignment and comparison groups. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T7#GNS224_U1_T7_h3)

question: Why might a nurse researcher choose a quasi-experimental design over a true experimental design?

options.A: Quasi-experimental studies completely eliminate all threats to internal validity
options.B: Random assignment of patients to groups may be practically or ethically impossible
options.C: Quasi-experimental studies require no statistical analysis
options.D: True experiments are restricted by law in most healthcare settings

explanation: Clinical realities often prevent random assignment, such as when evaluating existing hospital units or community-wide interventions. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T7#GNS224_U1_T7_h3)

question: What is a dependent variable in a clinical experiment?

options.A: The intervention or treatment applied by the researcher
options.B: The measured clinical outcome or response being observed
options.C: An unmeasured confounding factor in the hospital environment
options.D: The method used to select participants from a population

explanation: The dependent variable represents what is being measured to see if the independent variable had an effect. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T7#GNS224_U1_T7_h4)

question: A researcher studies how a new handwashing technique affects bacterial count on nurses' hands. What represents the independent variable?

options.A: The brand of soap used in the control sink
options.B: The specific handwashing technique introduced
options.C: The bacterial count measured after washing
options.D: The number of participating nurses

explanation: The independent variable is the manipulated treatment or protocol being tested for its effect on the outcome. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T7#GNS224_U1_T7_h4)

question: What does internal validity refer to in an experimental study?

options.A: The accuracy of the laboratory equipment used to measure biological samples
options.B: Whether participants answered survey questions honestly
options.C: The degree to which study results can be generalized to other hospitals
options.D: Whether the independent variable truly caused the observed change in the dependent variable

explanation: Internal validity evaluates confidence that the intervention itself produced the outcome rather than extraneous variables. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T7#GNS224_U1_T7_h5)

question: Which scenario represents a threat to external validity?

options.A: A medication trial conducted exclusively on healthy young males fails to predict how elderly female patients will respond
options.B: Participants in a weight loss study drop out before the final measurement is taken
options.C: A faulty blood pressure cuff gives erratic readings during the post-test phase
options.D: Patients improve simply because they know they are being observed in a study

explanation: External validity is compromised when findings from a narrow sample cannot be safely applied to the wider patient population. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T7#GNS224_U1_T7_h5)

question: What is the very first step a nurse researcher must take when planning an experimental study?

options.A: Formulate a specific research question and hypothesis
options.B: Submit the final manuscript to a journal
options.C: Recruit participants from the outpatient clinic
options.D: Purchase data analysis software licenses

explanation: All research begins with defining a clear question and hypothesis that direct the choice of design and methodology. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T7#GNS224_U1_T7_h6)

question: At what point in an experimental study are baseline measurements typically gathered?

options.A: Before the experimental intervention is administered
options.B: Simultaneously with obtaining institutional ethical approval
options.C: Only when participants decide to withdraw from the study
options.D: Immediately after the final data analysis is completed

explanation: Pre-test measurements establish a baseline before the treatment is introduced, allowing researchers to measure subsequent change. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T7#GNS224_U1_T7_h6)
